vignette:
Fatima is 77 years old. She sits at a small desk in her apartment, a stack of algebra worksheets beside her neatly sharpened pencils. She is tutoring a 14-year-old boy named Amir over video call, her voice steady and patient. But she keeps the camera angle deliberately tight so he cannot see the window behind her. She has not opened the curtains in seven years.

The story begins in a different kitchen, in a different country. Fatima remembers the morning of the day that ended her former life. She was 64 then, a retired school principal, still living in her childhood home in a city that had become a war zone. She was making tea when the first shell hit three blocks away. The windows rattled, but she did not leave. She had survived months of shelling. She thought she was used to it.

Then came the afternoon of the marketplace. She had gone to buy vegetables for her nephew’s wedding dinner. She was selecting eggplants when the second blast came—closer, much closer. The sound was not a bang but a violent tearing of the air itself. She was thrown to the ground. When she opened her eyes, the stall beside her was gone. A woman’s shoe lay in a pool of water and blood. There was a ringing in her ears that never fully stopped.

Fatima fled the country three days later. She carried only a small bag and her late mother’s prayer beads. She came to this quiet suburb, was granted asylum, and found work as a tutor. She never told her students what happened. When Amir asks why she flinches at the sound of a car backfiring, she says she is just startled. But her heart hammers for an hour afterward, and she cancels the next three sessions.

Now, in the present tense of each day, Fatima lives with the aftermath. She does not go to markets. She orders groceries online, even though the delivery fee strains her budget. She cannot tolerate sudden loud noises—a dropped book, a slammed door—without feeling her stomach drop and her hands shake. She sleeps in a room without windows, her mattress on the floor. Nightmares come most nights: the whistle of the shell, the moment of impact, the shoe. She wakes with her jaw clenched and her nightgown soaked through.

She avoids conversation about politics, about the news, about the country she left. When her students mention holidays or family gatherings, she smiles tightly and changes the subject. She has not called her surviving nephew in two years. She tells herself she is too busy, but the truth is she cannot bear hearing his voice, because it brings back the smell of the marketplace.

Her tutoring work is her only anchor. She takes it seriously, preparing each lesson with meticulous care. Her students respect her. She explains quadratic equations with a calm that belies the storm inside. But sometimes, when a student makes a careless mistake, she feels a flash of irrational anger—not at them, but at the unfairness of her own broken attention. She cannot remember a phone number for more than a few seconds. She double-checks every appointment three times.

She is never late. She is never disorganized. She is never anything but controlled, because control is the only thing keeping her from falling apart. She has not cried since the morning she left. She tells herself she is fine. She tells herself she is lucky. But at night, alone in her windowless room, she listens for the whistle that never comes—and waits for it anyway.
